title: Surface corrections and vortex energetics in the Thomas--Fermi limit of a self-bound unitary Fermi superfluid
abstract: We study a spin-balanced unitary Fermi superfluid bound by an attractive $1/r$ interaction within an extended Thomas--Fermi density functional. Its large-particle-number limit is the Lane--Emden polytrope of index $3/2$. We prove the leading gradient correction to the ground-state energy and strong convergence of the density amplitude. A rescaled surface problem predicts the next energy correction and the leading integrated density error. Matching a vortex core to the polytropic bulk gives the energetic threshold of a singly quantized central vortex, including the constant beyond the leading logarithm. Linearizing the same surface problem predicts a local energetic threshold for collective surface excitations that, in the natural TF frequency units, decreases more slowly with particle number than the central-vortex threshold. Radial stationary, spherical Bogoliubov--Poisson, and axisymmetric real-time calculations test the predicted energy corrections and vortex matching, and resolve finite-size surface-mode minima whose approach to the continuum surface coefficient is followed to $N\simeq4\times10^6$. For the reference gradient coefficient the vortex constant is $c_1=-0.535$, and the surface Landau scale is $1.417\,ω_K(\hbar_{\rm eff}^2/2R_{\rm TF})^{1/6}\propto N^{-1/9}$; sector energies at $N\simeq4.6\times10^5$, computed after the fit, agree with the extrapolated vortex threshold to $10^{-4}$. These results distinguish the accuracy of the Thomas--Fermi bulk from the gradient physics that controls the surface and vortex core, and separate vortex energetics from the open problem of nonlinear vortex entry.
summary: This paper rigorously calculates the energy corrections associated with the surface and the formation of quantized vortices in a unitary Fermi superfluid using the Thomas-Fermi approximation. By employing matched asymptotics and extensive numerical simulations, the authors distinguish between bulk physics and the critical gradient physics that governs surface and vortex stability. The results offer precise theoretical benchmarks for understanding superfluid behavior in trapped atomic gases.
main_problem: The study investigates surface corrections and the energetics of quantized vortices in a self-bound unitary Fermi superfluid within the Thomas-Fermi (TF) limit.
main_result: The analysis successfully separates the accuracy of the TF bulk description from the gradient physics governing the surface and vortex core, providing quantitative thresholds for vortex energy.
method: The work combines theoretical derivations using extended Thomas-Fermi functionals, matched asymptotics for boundary layers, and numerical testing via Bogoliubov-Poisson and real-time calculations.
model_or_system: The system is a spin-balanced unitary Fermi superfluid interacting via an attractive 1/r potential, analyzed in the large-particle-number limit using an extended Thomas-Fermi density functional.
key_observables: Central vortex energy threshold, local energetic thresholds for surface excitations, and the surface Landau scale.
important_parameters: Particle number (N), effective Planck constant (hbar_eff), and the polytropic index (3/2).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Thomas-Fermi approximation and asymptotic matching techniques; nonlinear vortex entry dynamics are noted as open problems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate density profiles for different angular momenta ($\ell$), and show the calculated surface-mode energy ($\omega_l/l$) compared against theoretical predictions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the TF limit and leading gradient corrections to deriving the vortex energy via matched asymptotics, followed by extensive numerical validation of surface modes and vortex matching.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous theoretical tools to calculate finite-size corrections (surface/vortex) in strongly interacting quantum many-body systems, which is crucial for understanding real-world trapped atomic experiments.
